newsitem.title: USA: IBM preparing employee buyout program.
newsitem.headline: IBM preparing employee buyout program.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp., in a move to rebalance its worldwide work force, is preparing to offer a voluntary employee buyout plan to a few thousand eligible employees, sources and analysts said Tuesday.

The computer giant, which is seeing huge growth in its services business, is seeking more skilled employees in its growth areas but does not need the skills of some employees in the slower growth areas, such as its maintenance business, analysts said.
The offer is expected to come this week.
A spokesman for the Armonk, N.Y.-based computer maker declined to comment.

The New York Times reported that IBM was considering offering a buyout plan to 3,000 to 5,000 eligible employees. But one industry source said IBM was trying to "flush out" between 6,000 to 10,000 employees from some areas of its business, such as maintenance and its European operations, while it adds in its fast-growing computer services business.
IBM has already added 10,000 employees to services, with plans to add 4,000 to 5,000 more during the remainder of 1996.

At the end of 1995, IBM had a total worldwide work force of 225,000, with 110,000 of those employees in the United States. That compared with about 256,000 employees in 1993 when IBM began a massive restructuring.
An IBM spokesman said the company expected its total U.S. employment to grow in 1996, but he would not give any specific numbers.
Analysts said IBM hopes its offer is accepted by some employees in European countries such as Italy, where local laws make it very difficult to lay off employees.

"What would make sense is for them to reduce the work force overseas, particularly in Europe," said Bob Djurdjevic, president of Annex Research in Phoenix. "It's much more expensive to do it there and it's much more advantageous for people to leave."

While the buyout plan and other possible inducements have not been announced yet, some industry sources said the plan under consideration may require that employees have been at IBM for at least five years.
"Some people with critical skills will not be eligible," said one source. "The goal is to rebalance skills across IBM."

Analysts do not expect IBM to have to take a restructuring charge for the move, because it said in its second quarter conference call that it has set aside $400 million for the remaining restructuring moves in the second half of this year.
But if a certain number of employees do not accept the offer, IBM may have to consider layoffs, analysts said.
IBM's stock gained 37.5 cents to $123.125 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
